utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kind of propaganda? Can you give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. (redacted), it is inconceivable how much very respectful people in Prijedor, professional people like doctors -- for example, you could hear Dr. Musta, that was a physician, a specialist, a gynaecologist, Mr. Zeljko Sikora, and it was written that he, as a Croat, was castrating women and newly born Serbian children, Serb children, in order to prevent further reproduction and further procreating of Serb people. There were also something against an internist and cardiologist Muslim and saying he survived all therapies, and it was said that Dr. Mahmuljin wanted practically to kill his colleague, Dr. Zivko Dukic, because he was all the time after a heart attack of the other doctor, he was on purpose giving him the wrong type of drugs, and had it not been for a Serb lady doctor, Dr. Zivko Dukic would have died. They said for Dr. Mirza Mujadzic that he was a dwarf-like doctor than Dr. Ali Cehaja. They said he was a doctor, he was only corrupt, of Ustasha origin. There had been very many such examples. I think they picked up on purpose people who were respected, because in Prijedor area people respect and believe in doctors; and if you say for two doctors, a Muslim and a Croat, and if you write something like that about them, then ordinary people -- I mean, it is very easy to say to ordinary people: "You see what kind of danger can be threatening you from the Croats and the Muslims".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to such attacks on respected Muslims in the town, what terms were used generally to characterise Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Fundamentalists", "Alijas", "Mujaheddin", "Alija Balija", "Ustashe", fighters and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the term "Balija", is that an ethnic insult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it a term used in polite company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to attacks on Muslims, were there other things which dominated the propaganda in the new Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such topics, that the whole world was against the Serbs, that media the world over were writing only against the Serbs, that the Serbs were a heavenly people, that they were a much suffered people which was armed, and they knew how to defend themselves, they attacked numerous western politicians and a very low ethical level falling beneath both the human and journalistic code of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was a curfew imposed on Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 2nd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were the hours of curfew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from 10.00 to 5.00 at first and then, as far as I remember, from 9.00 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did it become difficult for Muslims and Croats to travel in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What mechanisms were imposed to restrict the movement of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, there were checkpoints in all areas at all entrances and exits from the town and in the town itself and in different parts of the town, and then I was surprised, I was staggered, very surprised, when I saw a neighbour who put a white arm band, and I ask him, why; it had been announced that all those who wanted to go out and move about had to wear a white band over the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say "all those", do you mean every member of the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I mean the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was the Muslim and Croat community which had to wear the white arm band?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there a control of movement in the individual buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Individual apartments or apartment buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside of the buildings and in the apartments themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How was that imposed? Was there a register of some sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims were either given notices or were sent on holidays. They had no arms, no uniforms, normally in civilian clothes. They were then -- duty guards were organised for Muslims. They had to sit in front of the buildings and note down all those entering, who they were visiting, why they were going into the building, when they would come out, etc., with the ID No.; and in the evening they submitted these to one of the Serbs, to a Serb, responsible for a particular building. In my building the man in charge was a gentleman called

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about something you mentioned that was terminations from employment; did Muslims and Croats begin to be discharged or terminated from their positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that limited to people with regular jobs or low paying jobs? Which segment of Muslim society was terminated from employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at first they fired heads, directors, those who held some positions, and then immediately in May, Mr. Miroslav Turnsek, manager of the biscuit factory, was fired because the propaganda said that he had been shipping weapons from Croatia in margarine he needed to make biscuit and cookies in his factory. Then Idriz Jakupovic, a director of the Centre for Social Work, and others followed suit, but the first one to be fired was the Mayor of the municipality as they did not allow him to enter the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did local Serbs react to the continued presence of Muslims or Croats in their positions if they managed to retain those jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if they reacted and how they reacted, but none of the Serbs rank and file citizens in enterprises, in schools or wherever, when Muslims and Croats were given notice, they never protested or asked why, and in some schools there was even applause when the principal read out the Muslims, Croats had to leave the session and that there was no room for them in that company any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One thing I wanted to raise with you that you mentioned earlier: I had asked you whether or not people began talking about members of other groups or even reporting them to the authorities, and you indicated that that was something that happened after the takeover. What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, it sufficed for someone to call the police station and say, "My neighbour listens to radio Zagreb or watches HTV"; it sufficed for that to detain that person. Excuse me, another instance, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the bank, Privredna Banka, a bank clerk came, saw a Croat, Mr. Marijan Zec, screamed and asked: "Is it possible that this Ustasha is still working at the bank?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know Marijan Zec?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was he associated in any way with Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned an incident which preceded the attack on Hambarine. How did you learn about that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was listening to Radio Prijedor and Mr. Zivko Ecim was reporting about how Serb patrol had been attacked in front of Hambarine in a field, and he mentioned then that an incident had happened after the Serb had fired first. Then the ultimatum was issued that men, Muslims, who had provoked that incident were to surrender, and that was how I learned about it because the shelling of Hambarine ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long after the ultimatum did the shelling begin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One can see it in an issue of Kozarski Vjesnik. The ultimatum was very terse, but the Crisis Staff announced that they were cutting shorter, cutting the ultimatum shorter. I do not know the deadlines exactly, but I know that the deadline was very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned the Crisis Staff, do you know when that was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was established after the takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who belonged to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those whom I know whom I have recorded on the tape at the session, I know there was Mr. Radmilo Zeljaja, Slobodan Kuruzovic, Spiro Marmat, Simo Miskovic, Slavko Budimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before the takeover, was Slavko Budimir a prominent person in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there anything about his background which impaired his prospects for political success before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that some seven or eight years before that, perhaps, he wanted to take up a position, but he was told that he could not be appointed to that particular post because his father was a Chetnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the takeover he became a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and chief of the public security station, that is, head of all the security in the municipality of Prijedor instead of Mr. Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you when the attack on Hambarine began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on my way from my sister's to (redacted) in the yard and then I hurried home and I was at home and then we were absolutely flabbergasted. It is very difficult to explain to one who has lived in peace for such a long time and in such a nice way to suddenly feel the sound of heavy shells from Urije airfield and count up to seven -- I remember that exactly -- from the moment it will be fired to its hitting whatever because one could feel the sound. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I ask for Exhibit 79, the Prijedor map, to be shown to the witness? (Exhibit 79 handed) (To the witness): (redacted) are you able to locate Prijedor on that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you find the Hambarine area as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is Hambarine on an elevated portion of the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on a hill, on the way towards Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long did the shelling of Hambarine continue for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I know it was for quite a long time. I cannot say if it was three, four or five hours, but it must have been more than just a few hours. There may have been intermissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of an attack on any other part of Prijedor after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, the attack on Kozarac ensued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you point out where Kozarac is on that map as well, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Given the distance between Prijedor and Kozarac, is one who was in Prijedor able to see what was happening in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see people from Kozarac coming into Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were those people gathered at particular places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gymnasium sports hall, Mladost, in the centre of the town near the secondary school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you hear reports on Radio Prijedor about the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They spoke tentatively that roadblocks put there by Muslim extremists had to be prevented, that they had to use a tank sent there to clear it and then the posse of Muslim extremists began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is there any report about what had happened to the police at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that 13 or 14 policemen had been captured and liquidated immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you in Prijedor on May 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened the morning of May 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning of May 30th, I heard on Radio Prijedor that Prijedor had been attacked by Muslim extremists. It was described in detail from both sides; they had come from Hambarine across the Sana River, that they had attacked Partizanska Street, were moving towards the radio station, the police station, the town hall, the municipal hall building, but owing to the quick intervention and force of the army that the attack was rejected, that many were liquidated, some arrested and that some had fled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you stay in your home that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there any troops in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you taken from your home that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in other parts of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town itself, do you mean, or in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In other parts of Prijedor town, on May 30th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other parts of the town, I learned that afterwards there were major fighting in Partizanska Street which goes along the Sana River in Stari Grad, the old town, that is, in direction of the Sana and its tributary Berek, and that major fighting was between those attackers, as they call them, Muslim extremists, next to Radio Prijedor, in the secondary school building, near the police station and the municipal hall building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Over the succeeding days did you learn whether or not members of the Muslim community from Prijedor town were being removed from the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the attack on Kozarac I learned even that the Muslim population was taken to Trnopolje, rather, that the road was open for them from Kozarac to Trnopolje. Then a few days later we heard that over 30 carriages, that is, freight carriages with women and old people had been taken away in an unknown direction; and after the attack, the so-called attack, on Prijedor, from my neighbourhood, from my area which is Rajkovac, Skela, Stari Grad, many men were taken away and women and children also. They were released later. They were put in the Balkan Hotel. Some of them were directly taken to SUP and some to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack on Hambarine, attack on Kozarac and the beginning of the removal of the Muslim community from Prijedor, had there been announcements or calls for Muslims and Croats to surrender weapons in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were those announcements made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were invitations to surrender all arms, personal, that is, those legally obtained even before the crisis and the weapons of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did Muslims respond to that demand for surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... and even on the radio and television, Banja Luka radio and television, were shown various areas to show how Muslims were coming, surrendering their weapons on tractors, cars, trucks, or some other smaller vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted), we missed the first part of your answer because of a technology problem. The question was, how did Muslims respond to the demand for surrender and the beginning of your answer was, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They responded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did some members of the Muslim community go out in the community and encourage people to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember Dr. Esad Sadikovic, an eminent citizen who was a doctor who worked for the United Nations, and Mr. Dedo Crnalic an eminent citizen of the town of Prijedor, a sports executive, a man of integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They went around to urge people to surrender any weapons they might have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did those include weapons for which people had lawful permits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that include hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of that -- pistols even.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the people you knew who had weapons surrender them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of three cases in my building because in my area there was an office assigned for that purpose for people to come and surrender their weapons. My neighbours, (redacted) (redacted) went there and surrendered their pistols for which they had the licences before the crisis. They surrendered them in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why did the Muslim people surrender these weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were afraid, because they did not need them, because it was futile, it was of no use to have a pistol; and it was very dangerous because there were daily searches in almost every flat inhabited by a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was your telephone service interrupted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the interrogation at Keraterm. I was taken to Keraterm first and after that my line was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When were you taken to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long were you held on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For only one day for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What kinds of questions were you asked during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you abused or mistreated during that one day in Keraterm in June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Yes, the actual arrest had been unpleasant. I was on the pavement in the town and a car pulled up, and soldiers jumped out of the car and put me into it. They drove me to the military barracks and after that to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before you were taken to Keraterm, did you learn whether or not friends and neighbours in the Muslim community were being taken away from their homes and disappearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. That was the usual, one could even say an everyday practice. You would just hear people say, "Yes, did you hear about it?" That is how we would discuss it among us. Marijan Zec, Sead Softic, Sefik Bijlkic were taken away almost every day regularly. So that almost every Muslim and every Croat at every moment would expect the same thing to happen to him. Whenever I would hear the sound of a car in front of my building, I started to dress.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You started to dress in anticipation of being taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is maybe not a nice thing to say, but my wife told me, "it seems as if you were just waiting to go".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you were returned home following one day in Keraterm, were you again arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you taken that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested by my neighbour who lived in the house next door. He was a professional policeman, by name of (redacted). He was (redacted) brother. He came in a Mercedes. I was as a civilian on duty in the morning in front of the entrance of the building. He told me that I had to go with him. I asked him, "Where to?" and he said, "To Omarska".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You have just said that you were on duty in the morning in front of the entrance of the building as a civilian. I do not understand what you mean by "on duty".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us, Muslims and Croats, that lived in particular buildings, we were all obliged to sit during the day in front of the entrance of our house and take down the notice of all those people who were going in and out of the house and in the evening to give all this information to Mr. Egic, saying who came to visit whom, at what time and for how long that person stayed there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you like to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): (redacted), after you were seized by the policeman (redacted), where did he take you --- (redacted), could you turn on your microphone, please? The interpreter in the booth cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Serbo-Croat]: He took me to the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Once inside the police station where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to a cell in that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you searched first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were whatever possessions you had taken from you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was particularly upset because they took my shoelaces off because I am no criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were other people in the cell when you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was only one man by the name of (redacted). He was the owner of a restaurant in Prijedor; Albanian by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did other people join you and (redacted) in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With us there were -- we were eight together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the nationality of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was a Croat, his name was (redacted), an Albanian, and the six of us were Muslims, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were arrested in the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What time was it when you were finally taken from the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere past 10 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you receive any food or water during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At 10 o'clock or after 10 o'clock that evening what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They opened the door of the cell, this is a metal door, they started to shout, saying, "Get out, you Ustashas and fundamentalists". They started swearing, beating and they ordered us to stand against the wall in the yard of the police station having our legs spread out and the arms against the wall. They were beating us, they swore at us, threatened us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did they use to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With police batons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were they swearing at you as they beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They swore our mother, our Ustasha fundamentalist or extremist mother -- very, very heavy words which this Tribunal could not accept as something that was underneath anything that could be spoken in polite company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then did they direct you to go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not tell us, but in the centre of the yard, some 20 metres from that wall, there was a special police vehicle open as a van -- we call it a black Mariah -- and next to that black Mariah there were two lines of policemen as in a gauntlet, and they ordered us to run towards the open door of that vehicle. We were running as fast as we could because they were beating us. Kasim Mesanovic fell down. He received a blow with a boot in near the eyes. Then we ran in that van. It is a very small space. We were full of blood, the eight of us holding our hands. Then the door closed behind us and we were taken in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When that journey was over where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the journey was over we found ourselves at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted), have you had a brief opportunity to look at the exhibit in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that as being a model of the Omarska camp to which you were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did the van stop when you arrived in Omarska, where were you taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same procedure again as when we were escorted from the police station in front of this wall here, here, here, the van stopped roughly speaking here. We were following from this direction and here, here. They ordered us out of the car and then in front of these walls here, we had to put our arms against the wall, spread our legs and then the beatings again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who was beating you this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were beaten by the people who were there at Omarska waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were you and the other prisoners beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were not only police batons now. Various types of weapons made from wood, then of wooden cane or something that looked more like a mallet, then a lengthy part in wood with various kind of pointed bits on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the persons beating you saying anything to the prisoners or yelling anything at them as they beat you and the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same thing again. The same type of vocabulary just in a different way, maybe in a more violent way, more severe, more offensive, just the nuances were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there ethnic curses against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Curses against Croats and Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the beating finished, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you point to the white house? I am not sure you can reach it completely but point to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here is the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you taken inside the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the second room on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were the prisoners already in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the nationality of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was their condition? What did they look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in a very poor state. For me who had only arrived there from what I could call normal life, it came as a shock to me. On the floor people, silhouettes, were lying, frightened people, piled up on one on the others, dark in colour, starved, huge beards, their eyes were like they were inside their heads. There was not a square centimetre of space there on those tiles. I had the feeling they were lying one on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you know those prisoners personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know where they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on I learned, from one person next to whom I lied down (whose last name was Sahbaz) that these were young men from Kamicani, Kevljani and from Kozarac who had surrendered to the Serbs, to the Serb army, at Mrakovica on Kozara mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Incidentally, do you remember if there was a man there with a hearing problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know whether his name was Deumic or Dautovic but I know that he used to work at the bakers' shop in Kozarac. His hair was long. He was not completely deaf and dumb, but he had a hearing problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you joined the others, the prisoners, in that room, what happened that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I calmed down, next to that man Sahbaz, next to a wall on these tiles a guard came and somebody said, and he said: "Who said who would be fleeing from here?" Nobody could say anything, utter a sound, even say that they would run away from there. Then he told me: "You, come here, get out". He told me to get out. In front of the white house there was fire there. They were around that fire, drunken, laughing, provoking, asking: "Where's your rifle?" "Which rifle?", said I, "I never had any kind of weapons, let alone a rifle." "Go inside" where I really could not wait to go back and calm down. Then underneath the open window of the white house I could hear sounds like a hog, then Radio Prijedor which is a provocation instead of Prijedor, then I hear: "Come here, come here, why do you pretend you are asleep? Come here to the window". I came to the window and I heard: "Pull out your head of the window". I pulled out my head of the window, and said: "Close the window". I shut it. Only my head was outside in the dark, and then I do not know who, but somebody put the point of the knife under my throat and then said: "Where's your rifle?" because they used to ask everybody where their rifle was. I once again said the same. Maybe I was a bit more open and I said: "No, I never ever had a rifle, nor I needed one". Then they asked me whether I had any money. In a small pocket I had ten billion of old dinars. I gave that money away. They asked me whether I wanted to buy cigarettes. I said: "Yes". What else could I say? They told me to go back to my place and after five minutes a hand came through a window and two packets of cigarettes were given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners from your room beaten that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did that start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It started, it is difficult to say exactly at what time because you were not even allowed to look at a watch, not move even slightly in order not to catch anyone's attention, but it happened in the evening, in the late evening, when Nermin or Ermin Foric was called out. I know his parents. I do not know exactly whether his first name is "Nermin" or "Ermin", but his last name is "Foric". He went out after they called him, and some 10 minutes later he came back with a huge bloody blue under his eye and his head was bloody, but he was wearing a smile and I could see that he was happy, he survived another calling up of names. An elderly man covered under a table with his body, his young son, and he exposed us his body in order to protect his son who was younger than 18 years. A bigger man was lying on the table. He was crying with pain, because he wore no shirt you could see huge blue bits along his body, bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners were called out of your room that night and returned beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe some five to six. As far as I can recall, because I might have even fallen asleep for a while, for half an hour or an hour. That was not real sleep, but the nature has its own rules and that is sometimes stronger than the feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did those beatings continue during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The next morning did guards come with any water or food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not in the morning. It was maybe noon already or thereabouts, because nobody dared to ask whether they could go to the toilet or go to drink some water. In the corner by the door there were two black plastic buckets, cut the upper part, and maybe some kind of motor oil was in there previously. One was -- both were used for toilet, one for urinating; the other one was used for water, and in that black bucket they brought water. We were thirsty and we were all holding, touching the edges of this plastic bucket trying to drink, and we were so desirous of drinking so that the bucket broke up, completely destroyed, and then on a newspaper a guard brought just crumbles of bread. Everybody was so hungry that they were even cutting the paper and the crumbles trying to find something to put in their mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to see who else was in the white house, in the other rooms of the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning I was able to see in the second room on the left that was opposite my room, I saw Husein Crnkic, a teacher of mathematics who was the head master of the secondary grammar school, then Asif Crnkic who was the manager of one part of the Omarska mine. I saw Marijan Zec, an economist from the bank and Sead Softic, an optician; Asim Kadic, the owner of the restaurant "Sport" in Prijedor. I saw in the first room to the right Esad Sadikovic; Sabahudin Avdagic, an engineer; Mehmedalija Sarajlic, another engineer; Zlatau Besirevic, the manager of Bosuamontaza company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to their professional lines, were any of these people soldiers at the time they were brought to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody, nobody. They were all wearing civilian clothes. Civilian clothes, shirts, t-shirts, trousers. Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were any of these men extremists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that any one of them was an extremist. I know them as ordinary people, people whom I used to meet daily in my town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did any of them ever express any interest or ambition to attack the JNA or Serb military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know completely but, as far as I know them personally, no, never. They never had such a desire. I cannot guarantee what somebody holds in one's head, but I know those people as being honest, good, not having any weapons, wearing civilian clothes, respectable citizens. I could never believe that they wanted war, extremism or to do harm to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality were these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marijan Zec is a Croat; the others were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was their physical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were worse. It was worse than my condition because I had only arrived, but it was better than those of a group of people I saw in the room where I was there. One could see some markings or some signs on their faces, either a wound or a bruise or a trace of blood, and what marked me most were their eyes, the look. Whenever I looked at some of them, even later, I had a feeling those eyes were not on the outside but somewhere deep, deep inside, in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also have a chance to see the first room on the left in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you describe what that looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a -- this was a death room, a small room, and the door was open, we would run out for food, and for short, brief intervals one could see. Then I saw Anes Medunjanin, a young man whom I knew from before, but I could hardly recognise him. He was not like other people with a lost face, but he was some kind of a heap, his eyes were peering almost. Everything was inflamed because of blows and he was kneeling near the wall. Then I saw Ekimovic, son of Omer Ekimovic, and called "Dado". I could see bloody stains on the walls that were dark in colour. On the tiles I saw puddles of blood. I saw something that a man never, ever wants to see again or to describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there persons other than Anes and Adnan in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I know those two people, that is why I mentioned them. Only later I learned who were other people there so I can tell you, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the condition of the other men in the first room to the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same condition in which I described Anes was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Adnan Ekimovic also have a relative in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. His father Omer Ekimovic who was in the second room on the left; whereas Adnan was in the first room on the left. I saw Omer when he was coming back from lunch. He was so fearful, but with this eye he was turning his head towards the first room on the left to see his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he try to communicate with his son or send things to his son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he try to get any food to his son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time when he would go to lunch, he would leave half of his bit of bread for his son, Adnan, and he would ask Eso Sadikovic, a physician, to take that bread to him; and later on at one occasion Eso said: "I went to give Adnan this part of bread, he is not there". Adnan disappeared. I cannot tell this to Omer. He did not tell him and some days later Omer disappeared as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the nationality of the men in the first room to the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first room to the left were people of Muslim nationality, but earlier on I had heard that Slavko Ecimovic used to be there. He is a Croat by nationality, but when I came to Omarska I did not find him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not there was a Serb in the camp as a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there was one, Darko, a young man, 20-ish, 25 perhaps. I saw him in front of the white house begging the guards to spare him, to say, "I am a Serb, let me go", and they were forcing him to repeat his entreaty once again to try to prove that he was a Serb; he was trying to, they laughed. Then he said, "Let me go. I am urinating blood. I cannot stand it any longer. I cannot stand up". Throughout the time they were sprinkling him with water, with a powerful jet of water, which normally was -- at normal times was used in the mines to wash tyres on those big trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was this Serb accused of somehow being sympathetic to or being in alliance with Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. They said that he was on the side of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As that day grew into evening, did the prisoners begin to prepare themselves for anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a fight, to be beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did they prepare themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to say "prepare themselves"; encouraged one another, whispering, and each one of us somehow tried to withdraw into oneself, to somehow reduce the size of one's body in this tremendous desirous attempt to disappear, to somehow shrink. Then if one managed to shrink then there was this illusion that you would be less noticeable and, therefore, less beaten. I have already described that father who covered his son with his own body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did a guard come to the door before the beatings began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A huge guard, a very tall guard came. I cannot really say whether he was really as tall as that or did he simply seem to us since we were lying on the floor all emaciated. He had a red beret and he took out a Kama which is an army knife and with the tip of that knife he began scratching on the glass saying, "There will be meat tonight."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners called out that night and beaten again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that continue through the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you also hear any sounds coming from the corridor of the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What sorts of sounds were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first laughter, shouts, ridiculing, then the cry of a woman, the entreaties of a male voice, then laughter again, sobbing, a scream. - then a guard came in, said: "I'm looking for two who are stronger". (redacted), was one of those. Then we learned that on the table put in the corridor rape was prepared of a young girl, and she was being raped by a Mehmedalija Sarajlic, an engineer, a Muslim, a respected citizen, a man of my age. They stripped her naked, that girl. They stripped him, forced him to undress, beat him. They wanted him to rape her and he was begging, imploring, saying, "She could be my child". I am really sorry for the coarse language, but then said to try to do it with a finger. He did that and it hurt her. She was screaming. He then gave it up completely. They beat him. He had a weak heart. In the morning when were taken out six by six to the loo, to the left of the white house to a lawn, I saw Mehmedalija Sarajlic's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long were you held in the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two nights and two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you moved to after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was the interrogation conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The interrogation was conducted on the upper floor of this building here; in the offices here. This is where one entered this building, up these stairs and depending on the room, which the prisoner went to which room, we were taken for interrogation. This was the entrance up the stairs and then here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What were you asked for in the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First they asked me why I had resigned. Again it was under some pressure, things like that. Then they asked me about specific persons. The interrogator was leafing through a notebook with covers, it had handwriting in it, as if incidentally or by the way, "Well, what do you think about Djedo?" I did not know who Djedo was. They asked him, "Is it Djedo?" About Mursel and then finally about Haris Silajdzic and Silvije Saric. I asked him in the end what will happen to us? He answered: "I don't know what will happen to us, let alone you."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the person who was interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not recognise him. There was -- we had heard that there were several persons apart from people from Prijedor, that there were some from Banja Luka, but according to what I learnt later this could have been possibly, I am not sure, Popovic, that is Jovan or Jovica Popovic, who also came from Banja Luka for these questionings. It was a man of a middle height, up to 40 years of age, balding. He looked very urban.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The pista. This is the pista, this was an area between this here building and this one. We were allowed to move up to this part, roughly here, so that one could get through, from here up to here and I was next to my friend by this wall here about 10 metres from the corner of this building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you estimate how many prisoners were held in the pista area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 600 and 800.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How much room was there for each prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As much as, enough to sit down or lie down, but with a part of the body over the body of another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did prisoners from on the pista stay there during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at night where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At night it was the worst because we were compelled to go to the restaurant, all of us, on the pista to this restaurant here, here, and to spend the night there and look at the area here on the pista. While it was, shall we say, comfortable in this small restaurant, we had spend, all of us had to spend the night there. There was barely room for sitting down sometimes, and in the morning once again running to the pista to find some space on the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did the prisoners do during the day on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the day the prisoners on the pista did nothing unless they had been called out for further questioning. They sat or tried to lie down waiting, seeking the permission of some guards to go to the loo, to get some water, and usually somebody would, someone with enough courage to ask to go to the toilet, they would take a group from this side through this hangar here, it is this building here, and there were some 700 to 800 prisoners and they would go through the hangar because the toilet was on that side. Then sometimes they would close it. They would allow one to go into the toilet but they would break in and start beating. There were often times people would avoid it who were afraid of asking for water or to go to the loo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you some questions then, (redacted), about the general conditions in the camp. How often were prisoners fed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once in 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How much food did prisoners get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As regards bread it was 1/8th of a loaf, 1/8th, and some fluid in a plate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You call it "fluid". Did you know what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More often than not I did not know what it was at all in terms of taste or its appearance. One could find some beans in it, so one could guess. Sometimes there were some potatoes, but more often than not I simply did not know what I was eating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How much time were prisoners given to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not more than a minute and a half to two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the prisoners go to eat individually or in groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regularly in groups of 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did some prisoners on occasion avoid going to get their 1/8th of a loaf of bread and whatever fluid was available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe there were at least not less than 100 to 200 prisoners refused to go for their meals daily because they were afraid of beating. I did that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners beaten when they went to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who would do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Guards escorting them or at the entrance into the restaurant or in the restaurant itself or along the line in the restaurant or at the exit from the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What nationality were the guards of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about facilities for personal hygiene? What was available to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing except water at times, not even the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did prisoners take care or attempt to take care of their personal hygiene or personal needs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At times it did happen that a prisoner, again through some guards, would get a plastic bag from home with a little bit of soap or chocolate or something else, but always small quantities, but regular invariably we never got anything, received anything from the authorities or in Omarska, we never got anything, any hygienic, any toiletries, toilet paper or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about prisoners who were sick or had suffered injuries, how were they taken care of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Eso Sadikovic, a doctor. He took care of them. He was also a prisoner in that camp himself, but he had no aids, no implements. He had nothing except an ordinary needle and thread.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did he attempt to bind prisoners' wounds with that needle and thread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on many occasions, one even with hairs. He tied hairs on their head to try to protect the brain of a prisoner; because his head was cut so much that he tried to do it in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In what position were the prisoners who remained in the pista during the day - standing, sitting, moving about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they sat. Perhaps from time to time somebody would walk two or three metres to someone. Some were lying down but free movement was not allowed. More often than not we heard orders when new prisoners would be brought in, and they were brought in daily, either on Mercedes or a van and it would stop here, in this part here, and they would take them out. We would be ordered then to turn to face the wall here along the pista. One day we were lying prostrate on the pista for 11 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This was July, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any shelter from the sun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. I mean how could we be shielded in the sun? Those were orders. It was an order to lie down. You were simply ordered to lie down and we would lie down and there was no room enough to stretch. So just as we happened to be in the position that we happened to be in, somebody's leg perhaps on my neck and my foot on somebody's stomach. If anyone moved there would be shots in the air. They were firing at pigeons above us. Once a friend of mine had put a sock here, to dry here in this wall here between the bricks, and as I was lying there a soldier from here fired at that sock. I simply felt the sound above me and bits of plaster, bits of the wall which fell off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there women in the camp, women prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my knowledge, as far as I know, there were 38 women.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you see them in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the restaurant. In day time they sat in the restaurant in a form of a corner. In this part here and this part there there were chairs and they sat all the time while some women helped in the restaurant. They washed dishes or passed plates where we would come there for meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that new prisoners would come to Omarska and arrive in buses or Mercedes on the back side of the kitchen building. What happened when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those here I could see them while I was on the pista and those who were brought by buses I could hear them, because I was in this room later and buses came up to here. But when they would take them for interrogation it was usually depending on the kind of prisoners. As they would wait for interrogation they had to kneel in front of this wall with their hands against the wall and we had to turn our backs on them, but we could hear the blows, sobs, threats. After interrogation a number of people would be thrown out on to the pista, sprinkled from the hose and be gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long were you held in the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten to 12 days. I am not sure, but roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that where were you taken and where were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to a room we called "mujo’s" room. The door was here on this side, then passing through the corridor and arriving in this part here; not upstairs but on the ground floor. Here was a window and I lied down along that window.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said that from that particular room you could hear bus loads of new arrivals coming to camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was sometime in mid July 1992. We heard buses stopping and then that silence set in in this room where we were 600 to 700 of us and I was beneath a broken window. Then terrible threats began. Unloading, they were not throwing them, they were not throwing people off, they were unloading them and we could hear: "Look at this one, he's got soppy shoes. Look at this jacket. Look at this football player. This one's got two fingers missing." Then the sounds of blows, sobs, "Oh mother". The sound from the outer side of the wall, beatings and we knew that new prisoners were arriving. We heard that most of them came from Rizvanovici and Biscani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As those prisoners were being beaten could you hear whether the guards were hitting them in particular places or throwing them against the wall in particular ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard the beating, blows, but how they spoke the guards, "Until you break through this wall with your head, I won't let you". I could not see what he was doing behind the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then you could hear the sounds of the prisoners reacting in pain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How often did new bus loads of prisoners arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After mid-July there was a period when they arrived often, and then in early August it stopped or end of July, but then we can come back to this later when buses came from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How many prisoners were in the room that you were taken to after the pista, the mujina room?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How much room was there for those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back to that room I tell immediately how much room there was. I could not even find a place to sit until a friend of mine, (redacted), suggested that we alternate, that he sits until midnight and that I then sit after midnight. Nobody could stretch out his legs or lie on his back. It was simply we were trying to manage as best we could, but we were patient and sometimes we would get angry if someone would put his foot on your face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was on the floor of the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were prisoners called out of that room that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, almost every night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did some of those prisoners return to the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of those who did what was their condition generally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More often they were beaten, battered, but sometimes they came back looking quite normal as if nothing that happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you called from the room at any point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 23rd July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken by Ckalja to a room which was from the corridor directly next to the staircase. Jadranka Kondic was there with Ckalja. There was another one with moustaches, round cheeks. They told Jadranka to go out. Told me to sit down. Ckalja sat on the table, the other one was standing, and they told me: "We have something to tell you. You are in the first category. Do you know what that means? Liquidation." I got scared and my head dropped on one side and I began sweating. "But it can be arranged", he said. "Money, German Marks, 10,000 German Marks." "I don't have them. I have never had that much money." I offered the garage, land, household appliances, everything I had. No. "Will you write a note, sign, give a telephone number?" They told me then: "We'll try to bring it down to 3,000 and you have eight days to find that money, that your wife find it." I was merely back and I was called out again. Kemal Pajalic first, a man who had never been in the camp; then I, Mehmedalija Kapetanovic, Hajrudin Campara and Asim Kadic. We were told to take our things and come out. When you are called out in this manner then you know it is liquidation. We were taken out to this part here and waited to see what would happen to us. Then I saw two prisoners being brought out of the white house, two prisoners bringing out the lifeless body of Muhamed Burazirevic, Braco, from the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Ckalja ever show you any confirmation of his claim that you were on the liquidation list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was accompanied by a short man in uniform; cannot tell you his last name for sure but I think his name was Prcac. Around the corner from this building at the very corner, I was called, and I was shown a piece of paper with a name and a surname with the mention "L", the letter "L".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did he tell you the "L" represented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant "liquidation".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the deadline expired, did Ckalja, in fact, return and demand his money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then he told me on that occasion, "I arrange with an inspector. We are going to give him 2,500 deutschemarks and the two of us are going to take 500. Run away, hide, do not go anywhere so that no one could notice you and when you would be going away, I will put you somewhere and we will see where you will get".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ultimately, when you were not able to come up with the money, did Ckalja return again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Every day I was waiting to be called. I was silent. I was not going anywhere. Very often I skipped going to meals, and then the date of the roll calls came deciding who was supposed to go where.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Roll calls for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the purpose of the third and the second category; the third category were the so-called inoffensive, which were put on the pista and which had to go to Trnopolje. The second category was supposed to go for exchange, and the first category for liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened on the date of the roll calls?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they call the roll on that day, everybody went out, lots of people went out, from my room either on the pista or just outside, but some 20 or 30 of us were not called out at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What happened to the 20 or 30 of you who were not called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You meant what happened? I do not know what happened to the others, but I saw a policeman at this roll call and he used to work in a butcher's shop, a chicken shop. As far as I know, his last name was Zgonjanin and his nickname was "Koka". I went towards him and asked, "Why am I not on the list?" and he said, "I am going to check that." He left, went upstairs into the room and came back an hour later. He called me and I saw I was the third person whose name was being, was added to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long after that was it before you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand quite the question too well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long was that before you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about an hour or an hour and a half or two hours before I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that when the majority of prisoners were taken from Omarska and sent to other camps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which camp were you sent to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, how did you go from Omarska to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the most difficult day in my life. Although I had spent 44 days at Omarska, it is very difficult for me to speak about that, I am sorry; I have to. They called us out from the hangar, that is here. We were all put into the hangar, all of us that were meant to go to Manjaca. They tried to organise a group of 30 people, but then they abandoned that and we thought that we were to be sent to Trnopolje, but when I saw that next to the buses parked there there were pit guards then the military escorts, I doubted that we would be taken to Trnopolje. When they started to load us on buses, I saw that we would not be going to Trnopolje. They put between 100 to 120 and 130 people on a bus. People were lying on the floor of the bus. They were sitting in between seats and, unluckily, I was sitting just in the first row in the seats just behind the back of the driver. My friend, (redacted) (redacted), was seated on the second seat on the right. The escorts were the driver and two armed guards who had automatic rifles. When we left Omarska, the first escort who was nearer was holding the automatic rifles some 10 centimetres away from me. He said, "Those who are from the town of Prijedor could raise their heads up". What does that mean? We all had to lower our heads down while we were driving on-- while we were on that bus. I could not do it really. I had to put the head on the back of the seat. (redacted) (redacted) and myself, we raised our heads. All the others remain in that position with their heads low. Then they started to criticise, how come we are there with them? "What are you doing here?" Rezak asked whether he could drink water out of a plastic bottle. He allowed him to do so, but at that moment a tall man with a beard, with a beard, jumped on the bus. He was armed. He had a red beret and he was holding a huge stick in his hand. He saw that Rezak was drinking water and he started to beat him on his head. As I was sort of shrunk there, I felt awful blows on the left part of my shoulder blade. I heard that that was the hottest day of the year, 36 degrees Celsius. We were all lying, seated, bent, without water, without anything. The drivers put the heating on. During the drive the people were saying, "How come you manage to capture so many of them? You are heros". They would answer, "Would you like us to take one out for you so that you can butcher them? Just choose." They stopped at some kind of restaurant and people were throwing bottles at us and stones. We were driven from some half past one or 2 o'clock in the afternoon up until 10 p.m. and this is 60 to 70 kilometres away. They parked the buses in front of the entrance of the Manjaca camp. The fronts of the buses were facing. I might have fallen asleep and I heard softly almost some sobbing. As I was turned towards the back of the bus I saw that they were beating Rezak once again. Then I felt awful pain in my back and my neck. I was hit with a baseball bat on the neck. I screamed, not, it was like a dead man's sob, a cry. As a kind of reflex, I stood up and I was completely shivering and I felt pain in every bit of my fingers. Then I sat down once again and turned as they told me, and I was hit maybe some 10 times more on my back. I thought they had finished. I was happy I had survived. In the meantime, I heard a cry by Nezir Krak who was outside. They were slaughtering him while we were being beaten in there. As the door of the bus was open, a soldier came dressed in a military uniform, a real one. He told me to go out, get out. Incredulously, I saw that. I wanted to say, "You have just beaten me." He told me to get off. I got off outside. There was a circle of eight or nine soldiers who started to beat me with various objects on my head. Suddenly they stopped, and then I heard the voice of Zoran Babic: (redacted) (redacted). I ran towards the bus, and I fell. I was stabbed in part of my belly. I went inside. I was feeling blood. There was nothing I could stop the blood, everything was bloody, my trousers, my jacket. Somebody called Sistek gave me his shirt so I could stop the blood and clean myself. Then I felt an urge to go to the toilet because of fear. I did not dare go towards the door. So I did it in that part of the clothes I had on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted), how were conditions in Manjaca at least compared to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were joking very often, although the conditions were atrocious, sleeping, just being without food. We said, "It is as if you were in an hotel compared to Omarska". I would have preferred to stay another four months in Manjaca rather than spend one hour at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few more questions, if I may, about Omarska? I am sorry to return you to those questions. Did you ever see any prisoner beaten or killed in Omarska for using a Muslim or Islamic word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw -- I was some eight or nine metres away on the pista away from Rizah Hadzalic, a man from Prijedor, who finished eating, went out of the restaurant, sat down and while he was eating a guard came by and asked him, "Does it taste well?" and he just in a very human way, he was happy that somebody asked him something like that, he said, "Thank you, bujrum". "Bujrum" is a word used by Muslims; it is an old word and it means "here it is" or "thank you", and then I heard an awful shout of anger by a guard and then six or seven others came and they started hitting him, hitting that man, saying, "You used the word 'bujrum' for us?" I do not know for how long it lasted. Then later on he splashed him with water, with a hose, and he was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Djedo Crnalic before who along with Eso Sadikovic went through the opstina trying to persuade people to disarm as demanded by the new Serbian authorities. Did you see him in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and we talked many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where was he held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was held in our room, and from it there was a small, a small room, with a window there, and there in normal times miners, workers in the mine, received, were issued, their mining equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a prisoner forced to drink motor oil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in July as I was on the pista, in this part of the pista, near the entrance into this building. I saw a young man whose surname was Crnalic, who had inclined this motor oil and drinking it and made strange movements as if he was flying, dancing. The guards laughed, encouraged him. After they took him to the white house and some half hour or an hour later one could hear a burst of fire and they said that he had tried to escape from the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you in Omarska during Petrovdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before Petrovdan did you hear any guards talking about the upcoming holiday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the court, (redacted) what Petrovdan is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petrovdan is an orthodox family holiday. In eastern orthodox believers, people of Serb origin have various holidays apart from Christmas, such as St. Nicholas Day or St. Peter's Day, and families can choose, I do not know on the basis of what criteria, may choose a saint to celebrate his day. Petrovdan, that is St. Peter's Day and Nikoldan are very important saints celebrated by orthodox. That is as far as I can explain. I am not a sociologist. I am only speaking from experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So Petrovdan is a Serbian holiday, a Serbian orthodox holiday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an orthodox, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you hear from the guards before Petrovdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Numerous threats, "Ustasha, when we come in in the morning, we say 'you'", and then we heard them say there would be meat for Petrovdan because they would roast us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the night of Petrovdan where were you held at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is inside the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, inside the restaurant building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: From that ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- were you in a position to see what happened on Petrovdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have mentioned a number of beatings that took place, both specific incidents and regular ones. Let me ask you this question. Did the guards operate in shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three shifts. Momir Gruban, and then Ckalja, Milojica Kos, Krle and Radic -- I am sorry, I forgot Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How often did those shifts change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Over 24 hours, as far as I can remember, they would change twice, that is, Krkan's shift when we expected Krkan's shift to come on, then we thought: "Oh, he will be here the day after tomorrow, so we may still be alive".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there some reason why prisoners paid attention to which shift was coming up next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Krkan's shifts showed open brutality. They were the roughest. They threatened, shouted, nobody could go even to get some water or to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to the regular shift guards, were persons from outside permitted to enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were those soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did they do in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was in the pista, I saw a group of four soldiers standing here, and watching what they did, simply watching. I recognised one of them. His surname was Baldic, son of Misa Baldic, a tall, dark young man. They never did anything directly. They merely watched, and another instance, there was one Suskalo in a black uniform with Chetnik insignia who went to Bijela Kuca and asked for Alija Ganic and Alija Ganic had never been in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: (redacted), I want to ask you now about the people who you saw taken from rooms and who did not return.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.
